# CB RULES for the character-artist (GENERATED 2026-11-21 by tools/slice_rules.py from CB_RULES.md; do not edit)
CB_RULES.md is the master and wins. This file holds the rules that touch your job. Read it instead of the whole book. If a rule you need seems missing, run `python tools/rules.py --grep <words>`; never read CB_RULES.md or SKILL_FULL.md top to bottom.

## RULE NO. 1: MAKE A RICK-QUALITY VIDEO. If this fails, everything is wrong.
- Every rule below serves this one. Following a workflow step, passing a gate or ticking a box never excuses a result that is below Rick's.
- THE TEST, on every picture and every clip before CB sees it: put ours next to a Rick frame of the same kind of shot (same shot size, same kind of place). Ask plainly: would this pass as a frame from his channel? Look at story clarity, world detail, light and shadow, reflection, colour, acting, camera.
- If ours is clearly weaker, it is NOT done. Fix it, or tell CB exactly what is still below Rick and why. Never present it as finished.
- If a workflow, tool or note leads to a result below Rick, the workflow is wrong: stop, say so, and use the method that reached the quality before (the airfield way).

## HARD RULE NO. 2: NOTHING GENERIC PASSES. EVERYTHING IS ULTRA DETAILED.
This is a gate, not advice. A frame that fails it is not shown to CB and not rendered further.
- **Generic = fail.** A plain box, ball tree, flat one-colour surface, typed font, filler word, star in place of a word, empty prop, standing or floor-sit pose where the story needs a real action, or a set that could belong to any film.
- **Every object in frame is specific to THIS story** and built from real parts, down to the small things: a wallet has pockets, stitching, a photo and flies that fly out; a board carries a real blueprint; a cart carries the ride's name; a loop under construction shows the crane and the missing piece.
- **Scale is checked:** trees about a quarter of the hero structure, a vehicle small around its rider, characters as large in frame as Rick's.
- **Poses are specific:** seated means a chair-sit with knees forward, sleeping means slumped with a tilt; body moves come from the trained motion library.
- **The test before CB sees it:** put the frame beside Rick's and name five specific details in every main object. If you cannot, or if Rick's shows a kind of thing ours lacks, it fails. Fix it first.
Full detail list: section 3, "PREMIUM DETAIL IN EVERYTHING".

## 11b. Token rules (every helper and the lead)
- T1 READ ONLY YOUR SLICE. A helper reads `rules/dept/<its department>.md` (made by `python tools/slice_rules.py`) and the files its brief names. It never reads the whole of CB_RULES.md or SKILL.md; when it needs one more rule it greps for the word. Only the lead reads the whole book, once per session.
- T2 A FRESH HELPER FOR EVERY FIX ROUND. A helper does one build or one fix round, then it ends. Before it reports it writes `STATE.md` in its work folder (at most 60 lines): what is built, the files and frame folders, the numbers measured, what is weak, what is open. The next round is a NEW helper that reads STATE.md and the notes. Never resume a helper that already did a round: each resumed step re-reads its whole history. (This replaces "one builder who stays through every fix round" in section 10.)
- T3 NUMBERS BEFORE PICTURES. Anything a script can measure is checked by a script that prints numbers: a figure cut by the frame edge, the named thing in frame on its word, floor share, saturation and brightness, frozen frames, loudness. A helper opens a picture only when a number fails or for the one final look. Pictures are looked at small: one sheet at most 1,600 px wide, at most 4 pictures per check round, never full-size frames one by one.
- T4 ONE COMMAND PER CYCLE. Render, sheets and measurements run from ONE script call. A long run goes in the background and the helper ends its turn; it does not wake up to wait, poll or look at a log. Every wake-up re-reads everything.
- T5 SHORT REPORTS, DETAIL IN FILES. A helper's report is at most 25 lines: done, numbers, weak points, files. Tables and lists go into a file the report names.
- T6 THE SMALL MODEL FOR MECHANICAL WORK. Rendering, joining, measuring, merging, fact checks, sound mix runs and file moves go to a helper on the smaller model (Agent tool `model: sonnet` or `haiku`). The main model is for story, acting, camera and look decisions.
- T7 A FRESH LEAD SESSION PER PHASE. Story, build and finish are three sessions, each started from HANDOFF.md. The lead never reads a helper's transcript and never pastes long tool output into the chat when a file path will do.
- T8 NOTHING BUILT TWICE. Before a helper builds a tool, a set part or a move, it greps `tools/`, `templates/` and the last episode for one that exists. Studies of Rick are done once and live in the rules and `references/`; a film does not study him again unless CB names a new question.
- T9 MEASURE EVERY FILM. At delivery the lead runs `python tools/token_report.py` and writes the totals into HANDOFF.md: tokens per helper, working hours, and the three most expensive helpers with the reason. A helper over 60 million tokens is a fault to explain.
- T10 NO WHOLE READS OF BIG FILES (V1.2). Never Read a file over 40 KB whole: grep, then Read with offset/limit. CB_RULES.md and rules/SKILL_FULL.md are printed with `python tools/rules.py` (--phase, sections, --grep), never read through. Code files (film.js, puppets.mjs, poses.mjs, library.mjs, char2d.mjs) are grepped for the export or key, never read through.
- T11 PICTURE BUDGET (V1.2). One contact sheet at most 1,600 px wide per look, at most 4 pictures per check round; Rick reference frames come from the board made once, never re-extracted per helper.
- T12 ONLY THE DEPARTMENTS A STEP NEEDS (V1.2). Before the gate: writer, camera-director, stretch builders. Other departments start only for work the board shows is missing; never the whole crew at once.
- T13 PATHS, NOT CONTENT (V1.2). A brief names files; it never pastes rule text, film.json or tool output into the prompt.
- T14 LOGS IN FILES (V1.2). Long command output goes to `_tmp/*.log`; only the summary lines (PASS/FAIL table, last 20 lines) are printed.
- T15 NO RE-READS (V1.2). A file already read in this session is not read again unless it changed.

## 11d. Solve it before it is built
- THE PICTURE PLAN, BEFORE ANY BUILD. After the script and voice the writer and the lead write `episodes/<name>/PICTURE_PLAN.md` in the format of `templates/PICTURE_PLAN.md`: one row for every thing or action the voice names, with the word it lands on, what we see, CLOSE / IN SCENE / NOT SHOWN and WHY in this story, the character's feeling on that word, an effect or gag only if this story's world gives one. CB approves it with the rough board (the one gate). Every row is a must for the builder; the line-check sheet is ordered by its rows.
- THE STORY DECIDES, NEVER A TEMPLATE. The plan is a format, not content: it is written fresh from each script and no row is copied from another film. A close-up goes in only where it fits the scene (section 10: secondary, must match the scene). "The voice says it" is not a reason; the reason is what the thing does in the story. Rick's numbers (96 % shown on the word, about 40 % close) check the total at the end and are never a quota per line.
- A LIBRARY OF PIECES IS TECHNIQUE, NOT CONTENT. Proven pieces live in `templates/pieces/` (built 2026-11-15 from the armor film: 17 pieces; 12 as code = hop, laugh, hit, double tap, live stroke, "got it", "told you so", the motion helpers, highlight of a part, fly-and-hit, burst of living things, time pass; 5 as numbers only = push-in, low-angle close-up, fly through an object, fly-land-rest, the "hundreds" count). Read `templates/pieces/INDEX.md`: each entry says WHEN IT FITS and when not, and what must change. `node templates/pieces/prove.mjs` and `prove_fx.mjs` must print PASS after any edit there. Known limits: the amounts of lean, arm and head inside a move are still the armor characters' and need an animator for another body; effect files give numbers per frame, the look is built new in the film's set module; the first film that imports a piece tests ONE move through the kit first (`templates/pieces/STATE.md`). A plan row names the piece AND what changes for this story (object, light, character). A piece used unchanged is generic and fails Hard Rule No. 2.
- AUTOMATIC FRAME CHECKS BEFORE CB SEES A VERSION: `node tools/frame_checks/check.mjs <film.json>` (built and proven 2026-11-15; about 40 s per stretch, quarter size, one process). On every camera rest it tests, per character: head with hat cut by the frame edge; the figure cut through by a side edge; set geometry between the camera and the face, or the head inside a mesh; feet floating or sunk. It prints numbers, saves one small crop per FAIL and exits 1 on a FAIL. Every builder runs it before reporting, and the lead before CB sees a version. A version with a FAIL is not sent, unless the picture-plan row says in words that the figure at the edge is meant (a CLOSE on a thing with a face at the edge); such a waiver is named in the report. Proof: it caught three planted faults (head cut 23 %, body cut 49 %, head inside the engine) and found the Chief's face cut in half at the edge of the chalk close-up in the approved armor film (S1 frames 184-205), which nobody had seen. Limits: three.js stage only, not a Blender pass; one character covering another is not reported; a moving character is exempt on that frame; tuned on two stretches of one film.
- A NOTE FROM CB IS CHECKED AGAINST THE PLAN. Was the row there? If not, the row is added to the film's plan, and if the kind of thing was missing from the format, `templates/PICTURE_PLAN.md` gets the line, so the next film's plan catches it.

## 4. Characters
- FACE SHADOW: THE DRAWN ONE STAYS, THE GENERATED ONE NEVER. The template's own drawn face shadow (char2d faceShadow) STAYS on every character (film.json face_shadow true or unset). What is removed is every GENERATED shade on a face: the kit's card_shade (amount 0 AND rim_amount 0), the far light, any scene or costume shade on skin. Confirms FACE SHADE: ONLY THE DRAWN ONE below. The kit bug that ignored a sheet's faceShadow is fixed (castkit + puppets.mjs, film.json key face_shadow). Second generated shade found the same day: costume_shade treated the outer drawn crescent and a white animal's body as costume and darkened them in a hard ramp; every film sets `costume_shade.keep_drawn_light: true` (kit film.js, default off for old films), which leaves every white and light-grey drawn pixel exactly as drawn.
- FACE SHADE: ONLY THE DRAWN ONE. The soft shade the character template itself draws on the face, which makes the head read as a 3D form, STAYS. Nothing else may put shade on a face: no shadow from hair, hat or brim, no costume shade on skin, no shadow cast by a prop, an arm or another character, no card light or scene light that darkens the face in patches. Where older lines differ (RICK EDGE SHADOW, the night line "the face goes darker with the scene"), this line wins: the face may take the COLOUR of the scene light, but only the template's own shade shapes it. Check on every sheet with the eyes zoom: a grey patch on a face that the template did not draw = fix before sending.
- NO COLOURED LIGHT RIM ON A FACE, NO HORIZONTAL STREAKS IN HAIR. (1) The kit's card rim (card_shade rim_amount with the sun colour, and the `far` light) painted an orange band on the hero's cheek at dusk. Faces stay clean white with only the template's own soft shade: set `card_shade.amount` 0 AND `card_shade.rim_amount` 0 and no `far` colour light for the cast in every place; the warm light is shown on the costume, the props and the set. (2) The costume shade measured its ramp per pixel row, so hair beside the white face showed horizontal streaks. Every film sets `"costume_shade": { ..., "smooth": 40 }` (kit film.js, added 2026-11-15; default off so films in work keep their picture). The hair library's own curls and strands stay. Check: the face-and-hair zoom on the first frame of every new character.
- Only the locked 2D vector cast, four locked views. Flat cards, no soft 3D bodies.
- Heads pure WHITE in the finished Blender frame, never grey: the head is fully self-lit (card_emit 1.0, gain 1.3; measured face white 245+ of 255; CB asked twice), the scene light must not dim it. LOCKED 2026-11-11 15:30 Bangkok: CB compared self-lit white (v5, plus the white-head mask pass after the grade, 255 of 255) with heads lit by Blender light (grey-blue from the sky) and chose: "self lit is better". Do not let scene light shade the heads.
- RICK EDGE SHADOW on every head and body: a soft grey gradient just inside the outline, strongest on the side away from the light; the middle of the face stays pure white. Made by edge_shadow.py on the card, not drawn into the face.
- One view per character: side body = side hair and hat too. ("the look is from side. but the hair is front side")
- Facial hair where it grows: moustache above the mouth, beard on the chin. ("beard but its under mouth... not make sense")
- Legs and limbs one colour; no shoes. No faces with drawn text.
- STANDARD CHARACTER TEMPLATE v11 (LOCKED CB 2026-11-11 22:09: "Lock this as standard template"): every character is drawn on it. Full rules 6-17 in templates/vector2d_characters/VIEW_RULES.md; approved sheet views_golden/APPROVED_character_views_v7.png.
- LINE SHADOW COMES FROM THE LIGHT SOURCE: outlines thin on the lit side, heavy on the opposite side and the bottom edge, head and body; the lit side is the side the face looks to. ("Line shadow change from source light")
- LEG AND FEET DIRECTION DEPENDS ON THE CAMERA VIEW ANGLE: front toes 45 deg down-out, 3/4 toes 45 deg down to the facing side, side flat L feet forward, back toes 45 deg out and up. ("leg and feet direction depends on camera view angle")
- LIMBS ACT LIKE HUMAN LIMBS: bend only at real joints and only the way a person's can (elbows back, knees forward), can do everything a person does, hands and feet end ON what they touch. ("All limbs are acting like human limbs can move and do everything")
- Face 3D shadow is now drawn by the template (soft light grey on the side away from the light). In the Blender look do not stack a second head shadow from edge_shadow.py on top: check the head on the first look frame of each new episode.
- NO HAT OR HAIR BRIM SHADOW ON FACES: faces stay clean white under caps, hats and hair, as in Rick's films. The kit's brim shadow (film.js shadedTexture hat_shadow, 30 % darker, streaky) is off: default 0 in templates/threejs_film/film.js since 2026-11-12; patched kit copies in episodes set card_shade "hat_shadow": 0. Lock cards exported before that must be exported again. The template's thin soft side crescent on the face stays. Proof: project files episodes/roller-coaster/blender_check_2026-11-12/eye_shadow_before_after.png.
- COSTUME, HEADWEAR AND CLOTH ACCESSORIES GET A DARKER SHADOW SIDE: every outfit, hat, helmet, hood, scarf, bag, belt, cape and other cloth accessory has a clearly darker shade on the side away from the scene's key light (same direction as the face's soft 3D shadow), so it reads as a 3D form in the scene light. It sits next to NO HAT OR HAIR BRIM SHADOW ON FACES: the dark side is ON the costume and headwear themselves, never a shadow band cast onto the face. It is a shade, not a texture or line finish (CAUTION ON CHARACTERS still applies). Each thread shows CB a before and after on its cast before using it in a film. APPROVED BUILD (CB 2026-11-13 02:12 Bangkok on the cart army before/after: "exept for the face"): kit film.js key costume_shade (amount .45, start .35, cool .15; skips ink and skin, follows the view side), source project files episodes/cart-army/kit_patch/film_costume_shade.js; faces never get it.
- TEMPLATE v12 LOCKED: hats, hair, fur, ears, snouts and tails turn with the view; hair colour, highlights, lines and hair ties the same in every view; back clothing is its own design; back view = head fully covered by its hair. Rules 18-22 in VIEW_RULES.md, sheet APPROVED_character_views_v8.png.
- SITTING / KNEELING / CROUCHING LEGS (LOCKED CB 2026-11-12 00:10 "Ok lock", replaces the 22:28 thighs-in-outfit line; CB 23:44 "Dont create the other angle pants. The leg line stays black"): NO trouser or outfit thigh shapes in any view, only the black leg lines, drawn by the camera angle. Front and 3/4: the thigh points at the lens and is hidden, so the leg starts ON the lower body and runs down and out to the floor; legs read LONGER and wider because they come toward the camera, feet low in the frame in front of the seat (3/4: knees and feet turn to the facing side). Side: hip -> level thigh line forward -> knee -> shin straight down, foot flat L forward. Back: legs come out from under the body, toes point UP 45 deg and out (heel to the lens, "think logic"). KNEES and ELBOWS are never sharp corners, always a soft round bend ("Knee never eckig its have a bend"). Feet on the ground. Reference: Rick cashier frame, our match new-characters/style_change_2026-11-11/v23_bigger_fists/.
- ARMS (LOCKED CB 2026-11-12 00:10): arms exactly as thick as the legs; a small soft bend at the elbow so upper arm and forearm read as two parts; side view elbow bends BACK, away from the way he looks; raised/cheering arms leave the shoulder out to the side, round elbow beside the head, forearm almost straight up, hands at head-top height well clear of the head (pose cheer); FISTS BIG, about 2.5x the arm line (Rick).
- LONG CLOTH OUTFITS (LOCKED CB 2026-11-12 02:21; from Rick's How One Cart Stopped an Entire Army): skirts, dresses, gowns, robes, tabards and long coats keep the ORIGINAL body form exactly (shape, round bottom, outline) and add the long cloth as its own piece hanging UNDER / BEHIND the body, in front of the legs. Legs show only below the hem, never over the cloth. Standing: A-line from the body's own width, own colour, folds, dark or gold hem band, own back design. Sitting front/3-4/back: the cloth lies over the lap and hangs well past the knees (longer cloth hangs longer, max 60 % of the shin); side: along the thigh, over the knee, down in front of the shin. Length follows the form's legs (knee .32, mid-shin .51, ankle .69). Code: char2d S.skirt, long_cloth.mjs (gown, tabard, robe; doctor, knight, emperor), castkit spec.longCloth. VIEW_RULES rule 24.
- HAIR LIBRARY v2 LOCKED. Hair comes from templates/vector2d_characters/code/hair_lib.mjs (withHair). The outer hair line is thicker than the head line. Shading is soft (light crown, soft dark band inside the hairline, never hard bands), with 2-3 thin light streaks along the head curve on the lit side, one thin shine line, and a few thin tapered dark strands. Curls get light c-arcs; spikes are separate outlined locks. Head pieces sit on the hair, and under hats the hair still shows at the sides and back. Pick the style by the character's era, age and culture (each style has an era label). Full text: VIEW_RULES rule 25.
- HAIR v4 + HELMETS + MASKS (LOCKED CB 2026-11-12 03:23 'ok lock in'): hair_lib.mjs has 74 era-labelled styles (32 base, 28 by age/era/culture, 14 modern; coverings turban, hijab, kufi, sombrero). head_gear.mjs withGear(spec, hairKey, {helmet, mask}) gives 18 helmets/hoods and 13 masks. Pick hair, helmet and mask that match the character's era, age, culture and job. A helmet sits over the hair and the hair still shows at the sides and back; a mask turns with the eyes and mouth and never shows from the back. Every piece is built from real parts (rivets, straps, vents) with a soft gradient toward the light. Detail: templates\vector2d_characters\VIEW_RULES.md rule 26, pictures views_golden\hair_v4_gear\.
- FACE GEAR (LOCKED CB 2026-11-12 03:34 'lock'): face_gear.mjs withFace(spec, {beard, stache, acc, marks}) gives 13 beards, 9 moustaches, 24 face accessories, 12 tattoos and 16 face paints. Rick's way: the face stays white and the mouth is never covered; a beard is one inked shape hanging below the head from the jaw with short tick marks; glasses are thin ink rings. Paint and tattoos sit on the skin so eyes and mouth stay visible; tattoos are on the face or head only (limbs are ink lines). Pick pieces that match the character's era, age, culture and job, one clear signature per character. Detail: templates\vector2d_characters\VIEW_RULES.md rule 27, pictures views_golden\face_gear\.
- PLAIN OUTFIT = PLAIN BACK (LOCKED CB 2026-11-12 03:39 'if is plain the back need to be plain also no lines'): the back view of a plain body has no drawn lines, only the coat colour with its soft shading. Back lines appear only when the costume has its own designed back. Detail: templates\vector2d_characters\VIEW_RULES.md rule 28.
- THREE BODY SIZES (LOCKED CB 2026-11-12 19:24 Bangkok "ok lock"; replaces the four sizes; CB: "standard chnage to be thin. , fat is standard. extreme fat is fat/ use only this 3", "the body need to be littler longer too, with increse of body size", "now make the head also increase size by porpotion"): castkit spec.size = thin (the old standard width), standard (the old fat), fat (the old extreme fat). The old thin body is gone. With each size the body is longer (+20 / +55 / +90 px) and the head bigger (1.5 / 1.62 / 1.74); feet stay on the ground. Cast mostly standard and fat. Legs and arms always have the same line width (19 px) on every size; no film sets its own limb width. The other body forms are still only for when the story needs them (child, baby, ghost). Picture: views_golden\standard_body\APPROVED_three_body_sizes.png. VIEW_RULES 32.
- CHARACTER BIBLE, THREE SIZES: every NEW film takes its cast from code\bible_sizes.mjs, with bibleCast(n) for a cast of n or bibleChar(name) for one character. Sheets: sheets_png\three_sizes; outfits: views_golden\outfits\three_sizes. The old sheet files are unchanged, so a film already in animation keeps its cast. Characters keep the CLEAN look of the bible: no added texture, weave, stitch, fold-line or thick-outline finish (see CAUTION ON CHARACTERS in section 3).
- CHARACTER PRESETS, PRESERVE IDENTITY, VARY PERFORMANCE. Every character in every film is called by its ID (CHAR_001...) and built from its saved preset, never redrawn from a text description. A preset has 5 sections: 1 CHARACTER ID (id, name, style family); 2 VISUAL BLUEPRINT = the LOCKED layer (head shape, face layout, eye and mouth design, hair, beard, face fill, body size from the three-size bible, limb style, outfit key and colours from the 500-outfit library, approved costume variants, accessories, silhouette, line style, art style), linked to the exact master asset: castkit spec + bible_sizes entry for the 2D puppet, its golden sheet PNGs per view, and the Blender/GLB card when there is one; 3 PERSONALITY AND ACTING BLUEPRINT (the CAST_PERSONALITY profile: temperament, acting style, micro-behaviours, signature gestures, reaction speed, relationships); 4 ALLOWED VARIATIONS = the PERFORMANCE layer (expression from our face set, lip-sync mouths, arm and leg pose from the motion library, body rotation within the four locked views, action, emotion, camera angle, scene-light response, prop grips); 5 FORBIDDEN DEVIATIONS (never change head shape, hair or hair colour, face design, outfit silhouette or colours, limb style, size, line style or art style; no random accessories; no new outfit unless it is an approved variant). Hardest locked, almost 100 %: head shape, face layout, hair, outfit silhouette, main colours, body proportions, art style. PRESET COMPLIANCE CHECK before any shot goes on: silhouette, colours, head shape, face design, outfit, proportions, line style match the preset sheet in every view; the personality reads; only allowed variations changed. If not, revise before approving. Films already in animation keep their cast, now registered as presets. HOW WE RUN IT: the master registry (character bible) lives in the kit with the bible and outfit library and is built in the thread "Build Character ID system"; the character-artist owns the presets and runs the compliance check, the writer names IDs in the shot table, and the storyboard-judge fails any frame where a character drifts from its preset.
- ONE FIXED SIGNATURE DETAIL PER CHARACTER: every character preset (CHARACTER PRESETS, the Character ID) names one small, odd, fixed detail that makes drift easy to spot in any frame (a patch on one sleeve, a chipped tooth, a bent hat brim, a mole, one odd button). For the locked cast it is a detail the approved drawing ALREADY has, written into the preset, never a redraw; a NEW character gets one designed in and shown on its preset sheet before CB locks it. The PRESET COMPLIANCE CHECK looks for it in every view used; missing or moved = drift.
- SHORT COSTUMES BY DEFAULT: cast characters mostly in short outfits (tunic, shirt, jacket, vest, short coat) from the outfit library; long coats, robes, gowns and long skirts only when they are needed to identify the character or the era (a judge's robe, a royal gown, a monk, a Roman toga). When long cloth is used, LONG CLOTH MOVES WITH THE BODY applies. The writer says why in the cast list; the character-artist picks short first.
- SIDE VIEW SHOWS BOTH ARMS: in a side view the near arm is fully visible and the far arm shows only a little, partly hidden behind the body; never one arm only. The kit fix is made in the thread "Make hands grip items like real hands".
- HANDS GRIP ITEMS, KNEEL, LYING (CB 2026-11-12 20:55 Bangkok "ok", thread "Make hands grip items like real hands"; installed in the PC kit, view check 20/20, backup OneDrive RicksClipsBackup\grips_2026-11-12\before). HANDS ON OBJECTS (measured on Rick): the held object is drawn first, then the round black fist ON TOP, centred on the shaft, with a thumb and creases. The shaft comes out on both sides, and two hands sit on one straight shaft. Kinds (grips.mjs): pole, two-hand, shoulder, edge (a sign or box held by its front corners), behind (a shield covers the hand), hang (a lantern or bucket straight down), handles. Close-ups use realHand, a glove with wrapped fingers. Motion library held entries take wrap: angle or grip: {obj}. Poses: grip_pole, point, raise, swing, hang, shield, two, sign, box, shoulder, push. Never let a prop float beside a hand. KNEEL: the body stays upright, the thighs go straight down and the knees rest on the floor in every view; the side shin lies back along the floor. LYING: the body lies along a real line on the floor (act key lie_yaw). Each frame threejs_film/lie_cam.mjs picks the drawing from the camera: high camera = the top drawing along the line; body across the shot = the side drawing turned to the floor line; body at the lens = the feet drawing (big soles, belly, head peeking) or the head drawing. Heels rest on the floor, toes point up on the back, soles face up on the belly, no standing shadow. Poses: lie_back, lie_back_up, lie_front, lie_front_kick (on the belly on a bed, feet up), lie_flat. Never squash a lying card. Tests: threejs_film/test_grips.mjs and test_lie3d.mjs. (The cart army 3D-arm method in section 5 HANDS ON OBJECTS is for 3D tools; grips.mjs is the standard for card props.)
- GRIP LOGIC, SIDE VIEW BACK ARM, ACTING FACES (CB 2026-11-13 02:39 Bangkok "yes", thread "Make hands grip items like real hands"; ON THE PC kit: grips.mjs, char2d.mjs, poses.mjs, test_grips.mjs, test_faces.mjs; check_views PASS 20/20; backup OneDrive RicksClipsBackup\grips_2026-11-12\before_logic). 1 GRIP LOGIC: the same hand holds the item in every view (tools in the right hand, shield on the left arm); in side and 3/4 views the far-hand hold is drawn behind the body; poses kneel_work, kneel_hammer and kneel_hammer_hit (hammer head lands on the work); an arm never stretches past its length; the foot shadow stays on the floor. 2 SIDE VIEW BACK ARM (with SIDE VIEW SHOWS BOTH ARMS): the far arm is drawn behind the body from a shoulder a little behind the near one, and its forearm and fist show past the body; in a two-hand hold the far arm takes the hand further out; with bare hands at one spot the far hand sits a little higher and further; never drawn in front. 3 ACTING FACES: char2d FACES presets think, concentrate, aim, lipBite, holdBreath, browUp, frozenTongue, glanceCam, nervousSmile, proud (film.json face 'k:<name>'); the tongue corner and the glance follow the facing side (F.side). Check with threejs_film/test_faces.mjs and node tools/check_views.mjs before a render.
- HEAD ITEMS FIT THE HEAD (LOCKED CB 2026-11-12 19:24; CB: "some helm hair beard headpice are bigger than the head. please make them perfect fir."): a beard starts on the head outline and is never wider than the head. A closed helmet or hood shell sits on the head outline (half width 104 to 108 on a head of radius 100). Brims, horns, crests and cheek guards may stand out; the shell may not. No per-episode scaling of beards or helmets; fix the library instead. VIEW_RULES 33.
- HATS AND HEAD PIECES LOCKED: templates\vector2d_characters\code\head_wear.mjs, 34 hats + 16 head pieces, wear(spec, hairKey, {hat, pieces, hatCol, pieceCol}). Every hat FITS THE HEAD (crown never wider than the head, normal size; CB 04:09 "some are bigger than the head"). Every filled part has a colour grade, light rim on the lit edge, dark rim on the far edge, creases, one white shine streak, stitched bands and a soft shadow under the brim. VIEW_RULES 30, views_golden\head_wear\.
- MIX AND MATCH: every outfit, hat, piece and accessory in the libraries can be recoloured and combined across era and age; each choice must fit the story's period, place and character. Every new library item must take a colour option.
- OUTFIT LIBRARY: templates\vector2d_characters\code\outfit_lib.mjs + outfits_100.mjs, dress(S, key, {a, b, c}). Dress every character from this library first; an outfit is layers and small parts (collar, closure, chest items, armour, belt, hem, long cloth), fits all body sizes, and takes any palette (mix and match, fit the story). Every part carries the finish: colour grade, light streak, dark rim, crease lines, stitches, shine on metal. After any change run node code/of_check.mjs (0 bad). VIEW_RULES 31, views_golden\outfits\. The library is growing to 500 in this thread; more recipe files will follow under the same rule.

Same use: dress(S, key, {a, b, c}). Check: node code/of_check.mjs = 8000 renders, 0 bad. VIEW_RULES 31b.

No plain one-colour coat and no one-off costume code. Pick the outfit, colours, era and place that the script calls for (mix and match, but fit the story). If the library has no fitting outfit, add a new recipe to the library first, then use it.
  - Exception: an episode already in animation or render keeps its cast; new character kit changes go into it only when CB asks.
- LEGS AND ARMS IN SIDE AND 3/4 (CB 2026-11-15, five Rick poses rebuilt and approved; proof references/rick_pose_traces/ + references/reports/rick_poses_final_arms_2026-11-15.jpg; IN THE KIT: templates/motion_styles/rig.mjs drawPose and templates/threejs_film/puppets.mjs moveDraw). The NEAR leg (facing the lens) is drawn OVER the body, its line starting inside the torso about 10 % above the hem (hips 30 u in). The FAR leg stays behind the body. It is one tone lighter (#544656) ONLY when the scene has a light source (move P.lit or film.json act "lit": true); with no light source or at night both legs are the same ink (the default). In 3/4 and side the far arm goes BEHIND the body, its hand coming out at the target. 3/4 facing right: the screen-RIGHT arm is behind the body and the screen-LEFT arm hangs like a real person's: from the near shoulder at the body's SIDE, 35 u below the usual shoulder line so it starts clear of the head, straight down the side with the fist at -0.85 of the body half width; the far fist peeks just past the far side; facing left is the mirror. Side and 3/4 facing right: the screen-LEFT leg is the front leg (over the body), the screen-right leg behind; facing left mirrored. Heads are 1.1x wider than tall (char2d S.headW, default 1.1). Toes point where the character faces. Arms attach toward the middle of the body with a small elbow bend; a raised arm bows out with space from the head. A pose CB sets by hand goes in as exact points: feet[i].pts (+ curve for a rounded knee), feet[i].kneeAt, feet[i].over / far / ink / behind, P.arms [{ s, c, h, behind }], P.legW. When a pose correction misses twice, give CB the slider editor (references/rick_pose_traces/mk_editor.py) instead of guessing a third time. Front / 3/4 / back: the legs leave the body 2.4x the old hip width apart (Rick 30-39 % of the body width), the feet point out AND down about 25 deg, arms a little LONGER so a hanging hand reaches almost to the bottom edge of the body (armL x1.24, rest hand at bodyBot - 22). Proof references/reports/legs_spread_feet_arms_2026-11-15.jpg. CB said NO to tipping the body toward the lens (top wider) for now. CAST SHEETS USE THE SAME ARMS: bodies.mjs castArms gives every cast size the film rig's arms: hand at bodyBot - 22, side and 3/4-near shoulder 35 lower, 3/4 far arm behind the body; castkit sideFarArm puts the far fist at the body's FRONT edge (Rick never shows it past the back); rig.mjs and puppets.mjs side shoulder +35 too and keep armL from len0 so film arm length is unchanged. Proof references/era_match_sample/side_back_arm_fix.png, arms_moves_before_after.jpg.
- CHARACTER COLOUR MATCHES THE ENVIRONMENT: outfit colours are picked from or harmonised with the scene's palette (same saturation and grade family, never a colour that looks pasted on), and the outfit takes the scene's light colour, reflections and colour bounce (warm sun = warm lit side, pink room spills pink, a glowing prop throws its colour on the nearest side). The FACE does the same: its white takes the light's colour and the bounce (pink-white in a pink cell, cool white at night, warm white at sunset) and the face 3D shadow takes the shadow colour of the scene. UPDATED CB 2026-11-11 22:16 ("If have light source should have reflection on face. If night dark face also go darker"): the face follows the scene light like the outfit: a light source in the scene puts its reflection on the face (lit side, colour of the light), and at night or in a dark place the face goes darker with the scene. This replaces the 15:30 "self lit" lock for scene light; in a normal day scene the face still reads white. Check on the first look frame: character beside the set, does it look lit by that world?

## RULES FROM OTHER SECTIONS THAT NAME YOUR SUBJECT
### from 0. How to work (before anything is built)
- OPTIMIZE FIRST (CB 2026-11-13 20:5x Bangkok, bomber armor thread: "anything that help us to optimized and make it better is always first rule"). Whenever a film shows a way to make the pipeline faster or the result better, that improvement goes into the rules and the tools FIRST, in the same turn, before the next step of the film. Say plainly what went wrong, why, and what changes.
- Reference first: look at Rick's frames for the same kind of shot before building; never copy his story, characters or shots. Reference frames stay private.
- Show CB everything in the chat. No steps for CB at the PC. Only the final film is saved on the PC (and copied to OneDrive).
- Need CB's OK: any online/RunPod render, changes to the locked cast or MAIN LOOK. One Blender job at a time.

### from 2. Every picture (the mechanism)
- FRAME 0 IS THE HOOK: a character doing the strange act with the hero object readable. Never an object close-up, at the start or as the loop frame. ("start frame should be something noticeable, a hook")
- Literal sense: the picture must make sense for the line and the place. ("why standing sleeping that not make sense")
- Stay in the story's world: analogy scenes use the same period, place and cast. No modern set in a period story.

### from 3. World and look (Rick's 3D world, never a flat drawing)
- The WORLD is real 3D with real materials, light, shadow and reflection. Only the characters are flat 2D cards. A flat 2D drawing of the whole scene is wrong. ("oh no. what are you doing that is not like ricks")
- One strong key light you can see or infer (sun, window, lamp). Hard long shadows of characters and props; shaped light patches (window bars); colour bounce from strong colours; lamps glow. Light shafts only on the hook or a dramatic beat, soft and see-through. (Pink Prison)
- No ink lines on the world; ink only on characters. No film grain.
- Background blur: wides and mediums fully sharp; only close-ups get a mild soft background. Characters NEVER blur. ("background blur is too much", "characters never blur. always sharp")
- RICK FINISH (CB 2026-11-11: "apply everything that makes it more to rick clips style"; measured on his roller coaster film against ours, report https://claude.ai/artifact/H62bCh9DCKS58eqqD4vDVM):
  - Every character and prop throws a hard shadow on the ground from the one key light. No grey blob under the feet.
  - CONTACT SHADOW (ambient occlusion) where feet and things meet the ground: a small, soft, DARK patch right under each sole and under every prop, crate, stall leg and wheel, tight to the contact (about the width of the foot, fading within a few cm), on top of the long hard cast shadow, never instead of it, and never a big grey oval. Also soft darkening in corners, under overhangs and where walls meet the floor. In Blender the flat cards do not occlude by themselves: give each card a contact patch at its feet (decal or shadow-only plane on the floor) and keep EEVEE AO / fast GI on for the world. Check on every look frame: zoom on the feet, the character must look planted, not pasted on.
  - Surfaces carry real detail: wood grain and separate planks, corrugated metal, brick by brick, carpet nap, grass as blades with light and dark patches, dirt with pebbles. His fine surface detail measures 2 to 4 times a flat-colour set. No flat single-colour surfaces in a finished frame.
  - Hero objects are real models (BlenderKit first), not blocks: a car has a windscreen, bumper, chrome and wheels; a stump has bark and roots; stalls have goods.
  - Shiny highlights on chrome, paint, glass and lamps (about 1-2 % of the frame), and dark accents in the shadows; haze lifts the darkest 1 % to about 0.08-0.15 (measured on 25 of his films 2026-11-11, section 6b).
  - Depth: something big and close in the frame (a beam, a post, the edge of a cart), a pale far distance, corners a little darker.
  - Night is deep blue moonlight with small white-hot bulbs and ONE warm lamp pool. Never purple or orange ground, no oversized coloured bulbs.
  - Characters large in frame, hands doing the exact thing (wallet open in both hands, grip on the hammer handle).
  - Effects are real light and smoke (fire, sparks, glow streaks), not flat cut-out shapes.
- BLENDER = ONLY THE LAYERS IT DOES BETTER. For every film the coded three.js frame is the FINAL BASE: faces, cards, colours, light, framing and fx stay exactly as they are. A full Blender frame is no longer the final picture. Blender renders only MASKED LAYERS from the same lock camera, composited over the coded frame: metal reflections that move with the camera, wood grain and surface texture, bounce light, lit smoke and haze, light glowing through paper or snow, glints, motion blur on fast fx (never on characters). Each layer gets a before/after against the coded frame shown to CB; keep only a layer that clearly adds something, never one that makes the frame darker or flatter. This REPLACES the old Stage 2 "whole frame in Blender" step (step 6 above and SKILL.md FULL WORKFLOW Stage B are now "Blender layers"); BLENDER KEEPS THE CODED LIGHT and BLENDER NEVER WEAKER still hold. First used on the fireworks test (snow sparkle and burst bounce kept; lanterns, smoke and blur dropped).

### from 5. Movement and acting
- EVERY move comes from the trained motion library (templates/motion_styles), picked by action + feeling + energy + character. Always comedy. ("we did train body movement character movement you didn't use any of them here")
- CHARACTERS INTERACT, THEY DO NOT STAND NEXT TO THINGS (V1.2, 2026-11-21, from Rick's prison-tunnel clip: digging through the floor, climbing out of the hole, lifting the vault cover, stuffing cash in a bag, guards tossing the cell, a box set on the x-ray belt, things handed over, two men talking at a table). Every verb the voice gives a character on a thing or a person is a MOVE ON THE PROP: the hand ends ON the object, the object moves only because the body moved it (held, lifted, thrown on a gravity arc that lands and settles, set down and settling), and the other character in frame reacts (looks, nods, flinches). Use the interaction moves in `templates/motion_styles/moves/act_interact.mjs` (emerge, lift, grab, toss, place, give, talk) and `act_interact2.mjs` (point, open, knock, climbover, cards, shove, catch, duck, frisk, unlock, salute, pull, highfive, escort), played as `m:<id>+props` or the matching library move; a missing action gets a new move file in the same form. PICTURE_PLAN.md names the interaction (verb + prop + move id) on every such row; a named action played as a static pose fails the plan.
- Bodies never pass through objects. Hands END ON what they touch. Things are held, carried or pushed; nothing floats or flies in. ("treasure flying in that's also wrong")
- EXPRESSIONS: every character starts with a calm normal face. The face changes ON the narration word to fit the action or scene, never before, then returns to calm. Idle = blinks only. ("the expression made at the same time of narration, not before")
- CHARACTER ACTING, MICRO-EXPRESSIONS, PERSONALITY-DRIVEN PHYSICAL COMEDY: characters think, feel, anticipate and react; they never just perform a mechanical action. Every significant action carries ONE motivated human behaviour detail that comes from what the character is thinking or doing, never a random add-on: tongue slightly out of one mouth corner while concentrating, one eye squinted while aiming, biting the lower lip while working, one eyebrow up when confused, head tilt while thinking, holding the breath on a delicate task. Use facial asymmetry (brows and eyes move independently), eye direction and attention shifts, reaction delays, small wrist corrections and personality body language (tense shoulders, puffed chest). Write each gag as an ACTING SEQUENCE with times: how the behaviour starts, holds and changes, e.g. drilling 0.0-1.0 s studies the target, head tilt, eyes narrow; 1.0-2.0 leans in, tongue slowly comes out without him noticing; 2.0-3.5 drills, shoulders tense, tiny wrist corrections, brows furrowed; 3.5-4.2 drill jolts, he freezes, eyes wide, tongue still out; 4.2-5.0 slow glance to the camera, tongue back in, embarrassed. Comedy comes from tiny unconscious habits, awkward pauses, overconfidence and unexpected reactions (the nervous smile and pretend-nothing-happened after a mistake; the smug half-smile while pressing the wrong button). Faces sync with the action; no frozen faces, no repeated gestures, no random expressions, no robotic moves. HOW IT FITS OUR RULES: the face still starts calm and the big change lands ON the narration word (EXPRESSIONS); the behaviour detail plays DURING the action and the acting sequence; once a character has settled, DEAD STILL IN HOLDS still wins (blinks only, no idle breathing); the head wobble comes with each expression change. The writer marks the behaviour detail per action in the shot table, the animator acts it, and the character-artist adds any face part the rig lacks (tongue-out mouth, one-eye squint, independent brows, lip bite) as a request to the lead before the shot is built.
- UNIVERSAL CHARACTER PERSONALITY, PSYCHOLOGY AND SOCIAL DYNAMICS: act as a character animation director, comedy storyboard artist and performance specialist. Every character has a distinct, persistent personality that shapes how they think, move, interact, react, solve problems and behave around others. 1 PERSONALITY PROFILE: temperament, confidence, intelligence, competence, fears, motivations, emotional habits, strengths, weaknesses, quirks; kept across scenes unless the story changes them. 2 PERSONALITY-DRIVEN MOVEMENT: a calm expert moves deliberately and efficiently; a nervous beginner hesitates and overcorrects; an arrogant one exaggerates gestures; a sceptic uses restrained reactions, crossed arms, doubtful glances. 3 SHOW, DON'T TELL: personality through action, face, posture, timing, eye contact, gestures, object handling and reactions, not narration. 4 COMPETENCE AND CONFIDENCE: real skill is not the same as shown confidence (the expert works casually and precisely; the overconfident amateur performs dramatically and makes obvious mistakes). 5 SOCIAL DYNAMICS AND STATUS: how characters see and treat each other (admiration, scepticism, rivalry, disrespect, friendship, jealousy, intimidation, shifting status), shown through glances, spacing, interruptions, body language and contrasting reactions. 6 CONTRAST COMEDY: calm expert among panicking onlookers, confident fool beside a worried genius, the underestimated one who succeeds. 7 HABITS AND MICRO-EXPRESSIONS matched to the individual (see CHARACTER ACTING). 8 REACTION CHOREOGRAPHY: supporting characters are directed as carefully as the lead: true eye lines, reaction delays, facial transitions, exchanged glances, group reactions, all based on what they actually see or know. 9 EMOTIONAL CONTINUITY: emotions develop through events; no random expression changes between shots; the state and the relationships hold until the story changes them. 10 PERSONALITY GAGS from traits, relationships, unexpected competence, overconfidence, misunderstandings and clashes (see GAG SYSTEM). 11 SUBTLETY AND TIMING: not every moment is big; contrast movement and stillness; a small eyebrow raise can beat a huge cartoon reaction. 12 CHARACTER CONSISTENCY: each character keeps their posture, movement rhythm, gesture vocabulary, facial habits, reaction speed and social behaviour through the whole film. 13 VISUAL STORYTELLING: changes in relationship and status are shown in performance (the dismissed one earns respect later and is still recognisably themselves). For every scene decide what each character wants, believes, feels about the others and knows, and how their personality shapes their behaviour. Never give all characters the same generic expressions, gestures or reactions. HOW WE RUN IT: the writer writes `episodes/<name>/CAST_PERSONALITY.md` before the shot table (one profile per speaking or reacting character: the 13-point profile in short, posture, movement rhythm, 3-5 signature gestures, reaction speed, relationship to each other character, and how it changes in the story); each shot table row says what each character in frame wants, knows and feels; the animator picks library moves and timing from the profile; reactions are actions, so once a character has reacted and settled, DEAD STILL IN HOLDS applies again; the storyboard-judge fails panels where two characters react the same generic way or a reaction does not match what that character saw.
- NO TELEPORT, NO MORPHING. A character or prop changes place ONLY by a move the viewer sees (walk, run, climb, ride, be carried, be pushed), or across a real cut or transition that the story has there. Never pop, fade, blend or slide to a new spot inside a running shot. A change of pose is ACTED through a move from the motion library (stand up, sit down, climb in, turn); never a blend from one unrelated pose into another. Things do not appear or vanish in view; they are brought in, or they are already there when the shot starts. Check: play the animatic and stop at every place change and every pose change; if you cannot name the move that got him there, it fails.

- LIGHT ON THE CHARACTERS: every character is visibly lit by the scene's source. The side toward the sun, lamp, lantern or moon is brighter and takes that light's colour; a glint or rim on hair, hat, buckles and props from that source; hard shadow on the floor away from it. A card must never go dark because the light is behind it (in Blender the card takes light from both faces: diffuse + translucent, plus a small own-colour floor). Check one day and one night frame beside Rick before CB sees a set of shots.
- AIR LIFE AND WEATHER: every scene has air life that fits the place: dust motes in light beams, drifting haze, steam, smoke, insects or embers; weather where the story allows it (rain, snow, falling leaves, blowing sand) with surfaces to match (wet sheen, puddles, snow on roofs) and characters reacting to it. Indoors = dust in beams, smoke from burners; night = mist and moths at lanterns.
- LONG CLOTH MOVES WITH THE BODY: in every library move (pose m:<id> in films, rig_cast in tests) a long cloth (S.skirt) and a cape (S.behind) follow the legs the motion rig draws: upright the hem follows the legs; sitting it lies over the lap; kneeling, crouching, crawling or lying it wraps the legs and stops at the floor, never through a seat or the ground. No long bare legs beside a stiff robe. Cloth swings only during a move and settles within 8 to 12 frames; in a hold it is dead still. Keep it simple like Rick's robes. Check any new long outfit in walk, run, sit, kneel, jump, crawl and fall on the three body sizes before CB sees it.

- MOTION BLUR AND SPEED LINES: characters are NEVER motion-blurred (a new sharp pose every frame, as Rick); fast moves get 1-2 smear frames instead. Motion blur is allowed on the world and fast props only (wheels, thrown things, the background in a whip). Speed lines are allowed again (this replaces the 2026-11-10 "no speed lines" line in the kit) but premium: thin, tapered, few, soft glow or air-streak in the scene's light colour, short-lived, following the real direction of travel; never thick black comic lines, stars or clip-art bursts.
- FULL BODY FORM, NEVER SQUASH: THE CAMERA COMES DOWN TO THE CHARACTER. Whenever a character is in frame, the camera stands at the character's height: between chest and eye level for talk and acts, or low near the ground looking up for power. Down-angle from camera to the character's chest at most 10 degrees. Characters always stand upright (card turns only around the vertical axis, Blender LOCKED_TRACK lock Z); never tip the card toward the lens. High or top-down views are only for objects and places with no character in frame. If a shot starts high on the set, the camera cranes/pans DOWN to the character's height before or as the character enters. Check: compute the down-angle to every character per shot before rendering. (Magic bell: anim_hook AN "crane" {cam, aim, end}. The TRACK_TO card tilt is withdrawn.)
- CHARACTER TRAITS MATCH THE STORY + CARTOON POWER VFX: each character's look, outfit, build, props and way of moving say their role at first sight (clever judge = calm, tidy, sly half-smile; guilty thief = shifty eyes, sweat, hunched; brave guard = puffed chest). Feelings and acts are shown with cartoon effects in the story colours: sweat drops, anger steam, blush, a sparkle on a clever idea, a guilt aura or dark cloud, speed lines, shock lines, glowing eyes, stars after a hit, a power glow on the hero object. Every main beat gets at least one, on the narration word, built, popped and settled like the other VFX.

### from 6. Camera, transitions, effects, sound
- CAMERA: FLY, LAND, REST, FLY AGAIN (CB 2026-11-13 evening on the bomber armor animatic: "the camera movement is not what rick clips do", "too many cuts and just short camera fly, ricks clips have longer camere fly and stop then move. our move constant but in small moves only"; measured the same night on his roller coaster, cart army and railroads films against our animatic with one tracker, study in episodes/armor-no-holes/refs/camera_study/CAMERA_STUDY.md). This REPLACES every older line that says the camera never stops or moves 88-100 % of the time (CAMERA MOVEMENT ALWAYS, RICK CAMERA AND SET BUILD, the film check's rest and speed bands): measured with the film check's own line he RESTS 20-29 % of the time. His rhythm: a flight, a landing, a rest in which the picture itself changes (acting, an effect, a board filling), then the next flight. Numbers to hit: 2-3 LONG flights of 3 s or more per film (his longest 4.7-9.4 s), each attached to a moving thing or a line in the set; 21-45 % of the film inside flights of 2 s or more (ours 13 %); slow creep at most about 20 % (ours 39 %); the first flight starts inside the first second (ours 4.1 s); shot changes are 0.3 s dissolves with the camera moving through them, 12-13 a minute, and hard cuts 1-5 a minute, none in the first 20 s (ours 14 hard, 0 dissolves). Go from place to place by FLYING through the connected set where it allows it, and blend only where the clock jumps. CB's own words on it the same night: "camere stops often. but i think it mean is mostly constaty moing not cuting frame if is not ncessary only when it change to another different location. also transition in object thats introduce a new scenen is is alos good to have." So: the camera stops often, and that is right; what "always moving" means is ONE continuous camera that flies and rests without cutting the frame; a cut or blend comes only when the story goes to a different location; and a transition THROUGH AN OBJECT that introduces the new scene (the next place first seen inside a thing in the present shot, the camera goes into it) is wanted at those changes. TOOLS TO CORRECT before the next camera plan: the film check bands (rest share, speed median, travel p90 as a hard gate, no ban on flights over 7 s), the plan gate that forces a stop on every named word, a hook gate (first flight inside 1 s), and the kit must draw planned blends as dissolves, not cuts.

### from 7. Before sending to CB (sign every line by looking, not by the gate report)
- UNIVERSAL CINEMATIC ANIMATION DIRECTOR, 15 PERMANENT STANDARDS (CB 2026-11-13 02:23 Bangkok: "about 80% of that master prompt is universal... Keep this as Claude's permanent master instruction"; full texts kept in project files rules/CB_cinematic_master_2026-11-13.md). For every new script the crew works as a professional stylized 3D/2.5D studio and decides the visual direction, camera, environments, acting, materials, lighting, physics, VFX and transitions from the story itself: 1 character personality, 2 natural animation (anatomy, IK, balance, weight, contact), 3 facial acting, 4 dialogue and lip sync, 5 original context-aware gags, 6 narrative world building, 7 modeling and mechanics (primitives only for blocking, never as finished visible assets), 8 materials, 9 cinematic lighting (motivated key, soft fill so shadows are never black, controlled rim, contact shadows, atmosphere, a grade for the story and time of day; no flat even brightness, no over-saturated grass, no flat skies), 10 VFX, 11 cinematography, 12 physical consistency (no floating, sinking, clipping or foot sliding), 13 continuity, 14 stylized art direction (cartoon cast stays simple and clean, the world around it is rich and art-directed), 15 quality validation. Each standard already has its full rule in sections 2-6 (PERSONALITY, BODY MECHANICS, CHARACTER ACTING, DIALOGUE AND LIP SYNC, GAG SYSTEM, STORY-DRIVEN WORLD, PRODUCTION-READY MATERIALS, LIGHT, HIGH-QUALITY VFX, CAMERA); this line ties them together. Never force objects, effects, characters or gags into a scene that does not need them. Tools: three.js kit for set building, previs and the storyboard; Blender for detailed assets, materials, simulations and rendered passes; our own edit for sequencing (no Remotion in this pipeline). Never say an effect is built when the code only has a placeholder.
- SHOT-BY-SHOT VISUAL QA LOOP, 12 SCORES: every shot is rendered and looked at, never judged from code. The storyboard-judge scores it 1-10 from visible evidence beside the reference in 12 categories: story accuracy, camera and framing, depth, environment richness, modeling detail, materials, lighting, character acting, physical grounding, VFX structure, colour grade, continuity. Any important category under 8 = revise before the next step. Never claim an improvement without rendering and inspecting it, and say plainly what is still below the reference. These scores go on the PROOF PAGE.
- Premium detail: hero object, vehicle, structure, land and costume each checked at full size beside Rick's; lettering uses this story's words.
- 16-FRAME CHECK ON EVERY FINAL VIDEO: pull 16 evenly spaced frames from the finished MP4 (and the animatic) into one contact sheet and look at each for melting or duplicated props, a colour or shape change on a character or prop, a background that jumps inside a shot, a character sunk into the ground or floating, and a missing signature detail. Any hit = fix and re-check before CB sees it. It sits beside the RANDOM-FRAME STILL CHECK.
- PROOF PAGE with every delivery: each panel beside its Rick frame, the judge's score, the measured numbers, and what is still below Rick. No proof page = unchecked work, do not send.
- Tell CB plainly what is not finished yet.

### from 8. Build fixes learned (magic bell, 2026-11-11). Each one cost a re-render; check them bef
- A backdrop plane behind a window (sky, garden) must not cast shadows (visible_shadow = False), or the sun patch through the window disappears.
- Props that prove the story are built in 3D with their marks: the ink bell = glossy black body, four bronze handprints wiped out of the ink (palm + 4 fingers + thumb), drips at the lip.
- MECHANICS, BANNERS, EFFECTS (roller coaster round 2, CB's notes 2026-11-13 01:50 Bangkok: "summerize what you learn from this ... remember the camera movement"; full text project files episodes/roller-coaster/final/LESSONS_round2_2026-11-13.md): 1 cranks and handles turn with the fists ON the grip every frame: measure the fists per frame and drive the crank angle from that. 2 Banners hang still (stretched canvas on battens, no wind or folds); letters painted into the cloth material, never a see-through plane in front of a close character; nothing hangs in front of the words. 3 Mechanical motion follows the sound: a part that clicks 3 times moves in 3 steps with a small overshoot, never one smooth bend; when a part changes shape, hide every other version of it. 4 A person in a vehicle sits inside it: whole face in the windscreen, head under the roof; check the close shot. 5 Highlights on metal travel: they spread outward along the rail and slide, never sit still. 6 No effect freezes before the last frame: explosions keep growing and throwing bits to the end. 7 Wood reads as wood: grain along each part, knots, warm brown.

### from 9. LESSONS MERGED FROM THE SIDE NOTES (audit 2026-11-13; CB: "everything we learnd from th
- ONE VOICE, ALSO FOR QUOTED LINES. A character's quoted line is read by the same narrator voice with its own tone tag ([angry], [soft] ...). No second or third voice for characters, no cloned real-person voices. Reason: CB heard separate character voices and found them weird. Apply: the writer tags the quote line; the voice take is one speaker. Enforced by: writer check (one speaker id in the voice request).
- Footwear: no shoes; if a story ever needs footwear it covers the whole foot.
- ONE CHARACTER FIRST. A new outfit idea, body idea or finish is shown to CB on ONE standard character in the four views, and only after his OK rolled out to other forms and the cast. Reason: CB corrected each step live; a full sheet of a wrong idea wastes a round.
- The personality profile belongs to the FILM: it is written in that film's CAST_PERSONALITY.md under the character's ID. A profile stored in the preset is only an optional default. A costume for a new story becomes an approved variant of the same ID after CB has seen it.
- ANIMATICS ARE RENDERED AT FULL SIZE. The soft characters came from a half-size animatic scaled up. Render every animatic CB sees with `render.mjs --animatic --scale 1` (1080x1920).
- THE HIGHLIGHT IS LIGHT ON THE NAMED OBJECT. When a line names an object, that object's own surface glows in a flat saturated colour with a soft bloom for about a second, seen at first viewing. Metal gets ONE thin horizontal lens streak, never a cross (a cross reads as a star). No glow washed over a character; a face may change colour, only the face. Enforced by: film.json "highlights" (film.js: emissive tint + bloom, "flare": true).

### from 10. THE PROVEN BUILD METHOD (pin stretch test, CB 2026-11-14: "Yes, rebuild film". Proof:
- Every act of every character is an episode move written for that act (a moves file in the stretch's cast folder, loaded as `m:../../<file>/<style>`), drawn new on every frame: `tween.ones` true, `face_frames` 0. Count before any render: plain kit poses 0, frozen moves 0.
- Things that go in, on or at something FLY there and HIT: flight with a streak, a one-frame hit, a mark, a quiver, dust, and the thing that is hit shudders. Nothing just appears.
- CLOSE-UPS ON WHAT THE VOICE NAMES, AS A SECONDARY RULE THAT MUST MATCH THE SCENE. The scene comes first: its staging, its acting, the flow of the take. Where it fits that scene, the camera flies in and lands close on the thing the voice names, on the word, rests a beat and flies on; a named part may be highlighted with an effect. Never force a close-up on every noun and never chop a take into a string of inserts.
